> Verify that the application protects against LDAP injection vulnerabilities, or that specific security controls to prevent LDAP injection have been implemented.

* Difficult to understand/define action on below the statement
> “or that specific security controls... have been implemented.”

Which controls? Escaping? Input validation? Escaping? Parameterized APIs?
* “application protects against LDAP injection vulnerabilities” – is too broad and lacks measurable criteria. It should be described slightly like mentioning the LDAP escaping RFC rules like 4515 or other important implementations.

| **1.2.6** | Verify that the application protects against LDAP injection vulnerabilities, or that specific security controls to prevent LDAP injection have been implemented. | 2 |

The requirement was one of few that did not have any changes from v4.0.3. If to look at it, what the 2nd part of the requirement gives extra, that is not said in the first part?

So if we don't want to add implementation details and options, we can also live with just:

> Verify that the application protects against LDAP injection vulnerabilities.

If we want to have them, then

> Verify that the application protects against LDAP injection vulnerabilities. It can be achieved by option 1, option 2, option 3.

The way LDAP injection is shut down in code and similar is:

1) Parameterized / templated LDAP filters
2) LDAP escaping when a templated filter/parameterization is not available
3) Normalize to UTF‑8
4) You can also reduce the directory & query surface

...and I could go on.

The point is, **LDAP injection defense as a complete topic is quite complex**, and it makes sense not to try to get all the detail in the ASVS requirement and instead point to something like https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/LDAP_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html

“application protects against LDAP injection vulnerabilities, or that specific security controls... have been implemented”—is not about removing the goal of preventing LDAP injection but about making it clear and actionable. The current phrasing, particularly “specific security controls,” is ambiguous, leaving teams unsure about which controls (e.g., input validation, escaping, parameterized APIs) to implement or how to verify requirement.

> I propose slight elaboration, by mentioning RFC 4515 & 4514, alongside core controls like input validation, parameterized APIs, and secure configurations.

I think this is a vey good suggestion. In general, I prefer more details so developers understand what their job is.

> would like to know what's the definition or criteria to decide 'too prescriptive' in asvs context? so that this helps me to ignore few issues to report

This is difficult. In some places we are very prescriptive. In others, we are very general. It's something we usually talk over as a team of interested parties. But the trend is - to be less prescriptive.

> 
> I think this is a vey good suggestion. In general, I prefer more details so developers understand what their job is.

Thanks, Tomorrow, I will share some requirement suggestions that align with the highlighted expectation.

Here is the requirement suggestion:

**Verify that untrusted input is never concatenated into LDAP filters (RFC 4515) or distinguished names (RFC 4514). Use parameterized queries (ldap.filter.filter_format), validate input against strict patterns (e.g, [a-zA-Z0-9]+), or apply context-appropriate escaping (e.g., ldap_escape). If LDAP queries are constructed manually, escape all special characters (*, (, ), \\, /). Normalize input to UTF-8 (nfc) to prevent encoding-based bypasses. Limit LDAP query scope to specific attributes or subtrees, and enforce LDAPS with anonymous binding disabled.**

So this is a classic example where I think there is too much information here whilst at the same time [OWASP has a dedicated cheatsheet for this topic](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/LDAP_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html) which is referenced at the bottom of the page.

I would suggest keeping this requirement short and relying on the cheatsheet. Please do review the cheatsheet though @ajayojha to make sure it covers the points you make above.

**Short requirment suggestion**
First :

Verify that untrusted input is not directly concatenated into LDAP search filters(RFC 4515) or Distinguished Names (DNs) (RFC 4514). All input must be properly escaped using LDAP-specific escaping functions and validated against strict allowlists. Use parameterized LDAP APIs or query builders to separate query logic from user-controlled data.

Second :

Verify that untrusted input is not directly concatenated into LDAP search filters or Distinguished Names (DNs). All input must be properly escaped using LDAP-specific escaping functions and validated against strict allowlists. Use parameterized LDAP APIs or query builders to separate query logic from user-controlled data. disable anonymous binding, and limit query scope to specific attributes/subtrees.

"_Verify that untrusted input is not directly concatenated into LDAP search filters (RFC 4515) or Distinguished Names (DNs) (RFC 4514). All input must be properly escaped using LDAP-specific escaping functions and validated against strict allowlists. Use parameterized LDAP APIs or query builders to separate query logic from user-controlled data._"

Thanks, so I have some questions:

* Are the DN and search filter injection really two separate cases? From a quick review it looks like the only reason to mention DNs is if they get added to a search in which case this is still a search filter injection. Do you have a good example where the difference matters?
* "_must be properly escaped using LDAP-specific escaping functions and validated against strict allowlists_" - Both or is one sufficient? Do they fail the requirement if they don't do both?
* "_Use parameterized LDAP APIs or query builders to separate query logic from user-controlled data._" - Do solutions for this exist? I didn't see anything from a brief look.

> Are the DN and search filter injection really two separate cases? From a quick review it looks like the only reason to mention DNs is if they get added to a search in which case this is still a search filter injection. Do you have a good example where the difference matters?

Yes. Search filters and DNs each have different escaping rules defined in RFCs 4515 and 4514. Many libraries provide separate escaping functions for each. You can check [this commit](https://github.com/krb5/krb5/commit/e1caf6fb74981da62039846931ebdffed71309d1).

> "must be properly escaped using LDAP-specific escaping functions and validated against strict allowlists" - Both or is one sufficient? Do they fail the requirement if they don't do both?

From Defense-in-Depth perspective, both are required. If either is missing, the requirement is considered as a fail. Here are the popular packages example where both are applied.
[Dex v2.39.0](https://github.com/dexidp/dex/releases/tag/v2.39.0) – escapes and validates LDAP input.
[JupyterHub ldapauthenticator](https://github.com/jupyterhub/ldapauthenticator/blob/63faed592deb0173b8385463b9512ae7c0c0c055/ldapauthenticator/ldapauthenticator.py#L594) – regex validation + LDAP-specific escaping.

> "Use parameterized LDAP APIs or query builders to separate query logic from user-controlled data." - Do solutions for this exist? I didn't see anything from a brief look.

* **Java**: Spring [LdapQueryBuilder](https://docs.spring.io/spring-ldap/docs/current/api/org/springframework/ldap/query/LdapQueryBuilder.html)
* **Python**: [ldap-filter package](https://pypi.org/project/ldap-filter/)
* **Go**: ldap.EscapeFilter in [go-ldap](https://pkg.go.dev/gopkg.in/ldap.v1)

> > Are the DN and search filter injection really two separate cases? From a quick review it looks like the only reason to mention DNs is if they get added to a search in which case this is still a search filter injection. Do you have a good example where the difference matters?
> 
> Yes. Search filters and DNs each have different escaping rules defined in RFCs 4515 and 4514. Many libraries provide separate escaping functions for each. You can check [this commit](https://github.com/krb5/krb5/commit/e1caf6fb74981da62039846931ebdffed71309d1).

Ok, that makes sense.

> > "must be properly escaped using LDAP-specific escaping functions and validated against strict allowlists" - Both or is one sufficient? Do they fail the requirement if they don't do both?
> 
> From Defense-in-Depth perspective, both are required. If either is missing, the requirement is considered as a fail. Here are the popular packages example where both are applied. [Dex v2.39.0](https://github.com/dexidp/dex/releases/tag/v2.39.0) – escapes and validates LDAP input. [JupyterHub ldapauthenticator](https://github.com/jupyterhub/ldapauthenticator/blob/63faed592deb0173b8385463b9512ae7c0c0c055/ldapauthenticator/ldapauthenticator.py#L594) – regex validation + LDAP-specific escaping.

So to me it feels like validation should be covered by the standard input validation requirements so I would rather focus on escaping.
 
> > "Use parameterized LDAP APIs or query builders to separate query logic from user-controlled data." - Do solutions for this exist? I didn't see anything from a brief look.
> 
>     * **Java**: Spring [LdapQueryBuilder](https://docs.spring.io/spring-ldap/docs/current/api/org/springframework/ldap/query/LdapQueryBuilder.html)
> 
>     * **Python**: [ldap-filter package](https://pypi.org/project/ldap-filter/)
> 
>     * **Go**: ldap.EscapeFilter in [go-ldap](https://pkg.go.dev/gopkg.in/ldap.v1)

Ok that is good to know.

I would propose:

"_Verify that untrusted input is not directly concatenated into LDAP search filters (RFC 4515) or Distinguished Names (DNs) (RFC 4514). Use parameterized LDAP APIs or query builders to separate query logic from user-controlled data. Where this is not possible, escape content using context-specific escaping functions, based on the special characters defined in the respective RFCs._"

> So to me it feels like validation should be covered by the standard input validation requirements so I would rather focus on escaping.

How should developer may aware that he needs to add the validation like allowlisting with patterns like [a-zA-Z0-9]+?

If validation is skipped entirely, security can be weakened in edge cases. I will need to think about and share the list of these edge cases. Right now, it is more of a strong instinct based on experience, but I can research and confirm with concrete examples if needed.

> How should developer may aware that he needs to add the validation like allowlisting with patterns like [a-zA-Z0-9]+?

Input validation should be based on the reason for collecting the data item. If this data item is only used for ldap objects then the validation should be designed accordingly. If the data item is being used in multiple contexts then at this point the escaping becomes relevant.

Unfortunately, setting out the input validation required in every single use case is beyond the scope of ASVS.

the word “allowlist” and “validated” in many requirements, but for the LDAP injection these are out of scope. Is there any rule defined when they should be used in the requirements vs. when they should be covered by the general input-validation controls?
